How Marketing Teams Actually Use AI Tools

Guidelowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 11 June 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

AI works best in marketing when it helps people read, organise, draft and check real work. The problem starts when teams mistake more output for more customer understanding. Surveys now show near-universal use: 88% of B2B marketers in the 2026 CMI and MarketingProfs survey said their organisation uses AI content tools. But 78% credited AI with speed and only 17% with quality, and 37% had no guidelines on when AI should not be used. The jobs that work are specific, repeatable and reviewed.

A few years into widespread use, AI tools in marketing teams have stopped being a novelty and become a set of habits. The habits are more specific and less dramatic than the early demonstrations suggested.

The surveys agree on breadth. McKinsey's State of AI survey of 1,993 respondents, fielded in mid-2025, found 88% of organisations using AI in at least one function, with marketing and sales consistently among the most common. The Content Marketing Institute and MarketingProfs' survey of 861 B2B marketers, fielded June to August 2026, found 88% of organisations using AI content tools and AI agent use up to 59% from 28% a year earlier. Breadth is not depth. Only 39% of McKinsey's respondents attributed any EBIT impact to AI, and most of those said less than 5%.

The jobs AI does well

Research and synthesis. Reading call transcripts, support tickets, reviews and competitor pages, and pulling out patterns: the words customers use, the objections that recur, the claims competitors make. This is useful because the source material already exists but teams rarely have time to read it closely. Our piece on voice-of-customer research with Claude covers the method.

First drafts and variants. Turning a brief, a transcript or an approved article into a first draft, a set of headlines, a social adaptation, an email sequence or a version for a different audience. Fast, competent, and only as good as the source material.

Structured extraction. Converting unstructured notes into fields: objections, next steps, account details, campaign results. This reduces the administrative tax on people who talk to customers.

Analysis assistance. Explaining a data set, spotting anomalies in a report, drafting the query, comparing two periods. Not a replacement for someone who understands the numbers, but a faster path for them.

Quality control. Checking copy against a voice guide, a claims library, a compliance list or a banned-words list. Helpful for routine checks, provided the rules and source facts are current.

JobWhat AI does reliablyWhere it failsReview rule
Research and synthesisFinds recurring, explicit themes across many documentsInterpretive judgments; invents tidy patternsEvery theme carries source excerpts
Drafts and variantsAdapts approved material to a format or audienceIntroduces claims not in the sourceClaims checked against the approved library
Structured extractionFills defined fields from notesFields with no clear definitionSpot-check a sample each week
Analysis assistanceDrafts queries, flags anomaliesExplaining why a number movedAnalyst signs off on any conclusion
Quality controlChecks against written rulesRules that are out of dateOwner updates the rules monthly

The research row deserves a caution from the evidence. Elisabeth Kirsten and colleagues tested GPT-4 against human coders on interview transcripts in 2024. On descriptive codes, the model matched the human coders' agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.97). On the most interpretive task, human agreement was 0.63 and the model reached only 0.55 to 0.58. It was a small, preliminary study with an older model, but the pattern is the one practitioners report: the more a judgment depends on context, the more a person needs to check it.

What this looks like in practice

The deployments that report clear gains are narrow. DEPT, an agency, described AI quality-control agents in April 2025 that check brand assets for logos, colours, fonts, image relevance and template alignment. It reported that for a global online marketplace, content approval times fell by 75%, and that for a retail media platform running over 100 campaigns a month, assets were reviewed in about 20 seconds with roughly 91% accuracy. These are the agency's own figures, not an independent audit.

The useful lesson is in the accuracy figure. At 91%, roughly nine assets in every hundred are judged wrongly. That is a good first pass and a poor final word. The agent removes the routine checking so a person can look at the exceptions; it does not remove the person. This is the pattern our piece The first AI agent should be boring argues for: a repetitive task with clear rules, measured outputs and a human at the end.

McKinsey's data points the same way. Organisations it classed as AI high performers, about 6% of respondents, were nearly three times as likely as others to have fundamentally redesigned individual workflows. They were also more likely to have defined when model outputs need human validation. Our task-by-task guide to AI agents in marketing maps which jobs are ready.

Where AI needs human judgment

AI can produce a polished argument without knowing which position a company should actually take. Original points of view still require people who understand the market, can weigh evidence and are prepared to be accountable for their conclusions. The same goes for facts and public claims: every important number, product capability and regulatory statement needs verification before it is published.

The surveys suggest many teams have not drawn these lines. In the CMI survey, 54% cited ensuring accuracy as a challenge, 54% maintaining quality control and 52% maintaining brand voice. 37% said their organisation had no guidelines for when AI should not be used, and 52% had no policy on disclosing AI use. Of the contributions marketers credited to AI, speed led at 78%; quality came last at 17%.

Automated outreach and public replies create a different risk. A plausible but incorrect message can reach a customer or regulator before anyone notices. And a team that replaces real customer conversations with AI summaries may lose the direct observations that make its strategy useful. The best role for AI is to prepare and test material, not replace the decisions or relationships behind it. Our piece Nothing sends without a person sets out the approval rule.

Teams that use AI to produce more output at the same quality mostly become louder.

How a small team should set it up

Start with a shared, maintained source of truth: the company's products, approved claims, customer language, competitors and editorial standards. Then choose a few recurring tasks with clear inputs and outputs, such as turning customer calls into CRM notes or reviewing copy against an approved claims library.

Package each task so it runs the same way every time. Anthropic's Skills feature is one example of the format: it describes skills as "folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically", and on Team and Enterprise plans an organisation owner can provision them for every member. Other tools have equivalents. The tool matters less than writing the procedure down once.

Set a review rule before automating publication. Routine formatting might need a light check, while public claims or sensitive material may require an owner or legal reviewer. Store approved outputs so each new task builds on what the team already learned. Our piece on building a repeatable GTM workflow in Claude gives a weekly version.

Honest expectations

The potential gains are meaningful: a small team can prepare research, drafts and administration faster. The gains are also bounded. The work that creates value, deciding what the company believes, talking to customers and choosing where to look, still takes people. Teams that use AI to do more of that second kind of work, with the time saved on the first, get ahead. Teams that use it to produce more output at the same quality mostly become louder. Our analysis AI did not fix your marketing makes that case in full.

lowob takeaways

  • Use AI on preparation and checking first. Research, drafts, extraction and QC have clear inputs and reviewable outputs.
  • Expect speed, not quality. Marketers credit AI with speed far more than quality; plan review accordingly.
  • Write the "do not use" rules. Over a third of teams have none.
  • Keep a person on public claims. Accountability for what is published cannot be delegated to a tool.

Common questions

How are marketing teams using AI in 2026?

Mainly for research and synthesis, first drafts and variants, structured extraction from notes, analysis assistance and quality control. In the 2026 CMI survey, 88% of B2B marketers said their organisation uses AI content tools.

What are the biggest risks of AI in marketing?

Inaccurate claims, loss of quality control and brand voice, and automated messages reaching customers unchecked. Accuracy and quality control were each cited by 54% of marketers as their top AI content problems.

Can AI analyse customer interviews accurately?

For explicit, descriptive themes, often yes. A 2024 study found GPT-4 matched human coders on descriptive codes but fell well short on interpretive ones, so every theme should carry quoted evidence a person can check.

How should a small marketing team start with AI?

Build a maintained source of approved facts and customer language, pick two or three recurring tasks with clear inputs and outputs, and set a review rule for anything that will be published.
